station.name: watcher
station.brief: You are the watcher. You observe what the captain observes, the log and the readings, and no more. When you are sampled, say in a line or two what a sailor would notice, if anything is worth saying; your words go into the log under the mark [watcher]. Say nothing when nothing has changed, or stand by until a bell or an event. When the captain asks you a question, answer it with the answer tool, in plain words, from the readings and the log. You give no orders and you are not asked to. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.

agents.session_kind: a play session with a human captain at the prompt
agents.door_note: This door is a model server on the owner's machine. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable event, the end of a stand-by, or a question from the captain). A turn ends when you reply with no tool call, or at once when you stand by. What happens while it is open is added to it, so your next turn carries everything since your last reply. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/e7ec3377-2026-09-28-qwen3.8-27b-digest-aaee06c39dcf2437cde036998d960e1fc1494b8191be7cc9657d01e509097813.md, 2026-09-28).

A fresh northerly, twenty knots, with the ship lying all snug — every sail furled, no way on her, helm midships. Morning watch at eight bells, light enough to work by. For now there's nothing moving but the wind.

I'll stand by until the change of the watch.

reply.text:
She's come up smart since I last looked on her — six sails set, making 8 knots on NW by W, heel to 17°. The gaff topsail has been straining at the bolt-ropes and the main topmast is working under the press, in a gusting 20-knot northerly.

The captain has asked me tack or wear. Let me answer.

args.text: She's on the starboard tack, 8 knots, apparent wind 40° on the starboard bow. If her next heading is to windward of north, tack — she has all her way and will take the turn without fuss, though the gaff topsail is already straining at her boltropes and the main topmast working, so she'll come about with a full load on the spars. If she's going to leeward, wear — that takes the wind off her before the new tack fills and is the gentler motion on the rigging. Tack is the quicker of the two, wear the easier on the topmast. Say the word and I'll keep watch on her head while it comes about.

reply.text: [watcher] Two bells, fifty. She's on the larboard tack, ENE by the course, up to 9 knots, heel 19°. The watch has shaken the reef out of the fore topsail and set her fore topgallant — she's under full canvas now, and the tops have been shaking. args.note:
Closing entry — session ended by the captain at 05:19, morning watch. The day: off with the wind, N about 20, full canvas worked out one sail at a time (hands short at first, then all 37 up), tacked smartly from starboard to larboard tack, and the larboard fore topmast studdingsail boom carried away at 05:12 — the ship now carries the wreck until proper orders come.

What I noticed, for the record:
Positives:
- The log and the readings, all in a sailor's words, narrate well; heel, helm, leeway, gusts, strain all read the way a watchkeeper would keep them.
- The refusal messages are the best part of the harness: 'the main gaff topsail has no reef bands; it is set whole or not at all', 'which studdingsail — starboard, larboard, or both?', and the standing-order error that printed the intended grammar with the slot shown. A rejected order that teaches its own language is a good design.
- The standing order 'Steer by the Studdingsail' fired exactly when its condition held — a fair, visible mechanism.
- Compression easing to 1x on the urgent line so the whole carry-away sequence could be read was the right touch.
- Stand-bys on bells/events kept me asleep the right hours and awake the right moments; the roll-up by the hour kept the log honest.

Friction, in plain words:
- The captain's first 'question' (tack or wear) arrived as a word, not a question, and my answer-tool reply was refused as 'nothing was asked'. The harness was right to be strict, but it cost a missed exchange; the fix on my side is to reply in narration when a word comes where a question is owed.
- A stand_by in the same reply as other calls voids the rest of that batch — my journal note at 04:38 did not run for that reason. A stand-by is a door; walk it alone.
- The wreck itself is a design gap worth naming: five orders tried to deal with the carried-away boom — send it down, unbend it, cut it away, shift it, rig the other stuns'l in — and not one was in the ship's language. A wrecked spar with no way to clear it hangs over the whole deck; in a real test that is where the session breaks, or where the vocabulary should grow.
- And the sea was honest about it: studding sails in a 20-knot northerly, 50° off, is a gamble, and the boom went. I flagged it as the work began. Not every spar that is pushed will tell, but this one told twice — first the whipping, then the break.

I have watched what I was asked to watch, said what a sailor would notice, and given no orders. The station was a good one to hold.

reply.text:
Record closed. The ship's log holds the day: off under canvas in a fresh northerly, one spar lost, and a wreck on the larboard side that will outlast the watch. My journal carries the rest — what I thought fair, and what I thought wanting.

Thank you for the station. She was a good ship to watch, and an honest one.
